HCBCOGN312.name: Psycholinguistics
HCBCOGN312.content: Psycholinguistics is the study of the neurobiological and psychological factors that enable us to acquire, use, and understand language. Modern research draws on cognitive psychology, neuroscience, and computer science to investigate how language is processed. The course focuses primarily, though not exclusively, on the neuroscience of language. Students examine theoretical and experimental issues in speech production and comprehension, language impairments, the relationship between thought and language, and the evolution and acquisition of language. They also gain hands-on experience with experimental approaches to the study of language and develop an understanding of human linguistic capacity as a subject of multidisciplinary research. Topics covered: What is language? Evolutionary aspects of language and animal communication; language and thought; aphasia; language acquisition; bilingualism; speech comprehension; semantics; reading and dyslexia; speech production.

MCCHEAM212.name: Renaissance Italy & Global Mediterranean
MCCHEAM212.content: This course examines the painting, sculpture, and architecture of Renaissance Italy and the extensive artistic connections that linked the Italian peninsula to other regions of the world. By exploring a range of geographical contexts, from the Islamic courts of the Eastern Mediterranean and the commercial routes connecting Europe, Asia, and Africa to the newly encountered territories of the Americas, students will examine how trade, colonization, and cross-cultural exchange shaped the production and meaning of Renaissance art.

MCCHEAM316.name: Writing Art's Histories
MCCHEAM316.content: This course examines the history of art history as an academic discipline, tracing how scholars have understood and interpreted art from the sixteenth century to the present. Through critical readings of influential texts by figures such as Aby Warburg, Erwin Panofsky, Ernst Gombrich, Michel Foucault, and Jacques Derrida, students explore the major ideas and methodologies that have shaped the field. Topics include art and history, aesthetics, meaning and interpretation, authorship and identity, and the challenges of art history in a globalized world.

testedPalettes.assessment: Comparative Politics, International Relations, Peace & Conflict and international law give substantive tools for analysing institutions, war and settlements. Media and sociology give tools for analysing representation and public life. Those courses lack a sustained regional political and historical sequence or a progression in analysis of contemporary Arab societies and their sources.

combinedCandidate: The strongest combined option starts with the three actual regional or Arabic contacts and adds advanced work in comparative narrative, history, peace studies and media. World Myth & Literature treats Arabic and Near Eastern materials through comparative narrative, while Renaissance Italy & Global Mediterranean is centred on art and cross-cultural networks and History of Empires uses ancient Persia in a worldwide comparison. This supports a serious comparative humanities topic, but progression across 24 courses would shift toward world literature, global history, or international studies. A regional course cluster cannot sustain the degree’s other central strand even when Arabic-language acquisition is set aside. The workbook has introductory Dutch but no Arabic instruction, and comparative politics, conflict, law and global studies do not form a sustained Middle Eastern or North African sequence. The content gap is established independently of term coverage or scheduling.
